title: Hecuba
titleEn: The Fall of Troy and the Sacrifice of Polyxena — Metamorphoses XIII.399–493
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The victor sails for the country of Hypsipyle and Thoas to bring back the Tirynthian arrows, and with their return Troy and Priam fall together. Ilion burns: Jupiter's altar drinks the old king's blood, the priestess of Phoebus is dragged away by the hair, the Trojan mothers are hauled off as prizes, Astyanax is sent down from the towers where he used to watch his father fight, and Hecuba comes aboard last, found among her children's graves with a handful of Hector's ashes in her bosom. Across the water, the Thracian king to whom the boy's father had secretly given Polydorus to be reared cuts his throat for the wealth that came with him and throws him into the sea. On that shore the ghost of Achilles rises and demands Polyxena, and she is led to his mound and killed there, asking that no man's hand touch her and that her body go back to her mother unbought. The Trojan women reckon up how much blood one house has given, and Hecuba, embracing the body, begins to speak.

sentences.t:
Victor ad Hypsipyles patriam clarique Thoantis
et veterum terras infames caede virorum
vela dat, ut referat Tirynthia tela, sagittas.
sentences.l: The victor, to the fatherland of Hypsipyle and of famous Thoas and to lands infamous for the slaughter of their men of old, gives sails, so that he may bring back the Tirynthian weapons, the arrows.
sentences.i: The victor sets sail for the country of Hypsipyle and famous Thoas, lands infamous for the killing of their menfolk long ago, to fetch back the Tirynthian weapons — the arrows.
sentences.n: ‘vela dat’, literally “gives sails”, is the ordinary idiom for putting to sea. The island is named only by its royal house: the women there killed their men, and Hypsipyle alone saved her father Thoas, which is what makes the land ‘infames’, “of ill repute”. ‘veterum … virorum’ is split across the whole of 400, from its second word to its last. ‘Tirynthia tela’ are the weapons of the hero of Tiryns, and ‘sagittas’ stands in apposition, naming what they are: the arrows. The victor is not named here; he is called ‘victor Ulixes’ at 485.

sentences.t:
Quae postquam ad Graios, domino comitante, revexit,
imposita estque fero tandem manus ultima bello,
Troia simul Priamusque cadunt:
sentences.l: And these, after he had carried them back to the Greeks, with their owner accompanying, and the last hand had at last been laid upon the savage war, Troy and Priam together fall:
sentences.i: Once he had brought them back to the Greeks, their owner along with them, and the finishing hand had at last been laid on that savage war, Troy and Priam fell together:
sentences.n: ‘Quae’ opens the sentence as a connecting relative — “and these”, picking up the arrows, not a question. ‘domino comitante’ is an ablative absolute, a self-contained “with X doing” where English wants a clause: the owner of the arrows comes too. ‘manus ultima imponere’ is the idiom for putting the last hand to a piece of work. ‘cadunt’ is a historic present, dropping the narrative into the moment. Magnus prints ‘fero … bello’, “savage war”; some editions print ‘sero’, “late”.

sentences.t:
Priameia coniunx
perdidit infelix hominis post omnia formam
externasque novo latratu terruit auras,
longus in angustum qua clauditur Hellespontus.
sentences.l: Priam's wife, unhappy, lost after everything the shape of a human being, and with a new barking terrified foreign airs, where the long Hellespont is closed into a narrow.
sentences.i: Priam's wife, unhappy woman, after everything else lost the shape of a human being, and with a barking never heard from her before startled the air of a strange country, where the long Hellespont narrows to its strait.
sentences.n: The end of her story is given here, before the tale that produces it: she loses human shape, and the barking says what she became. ‘Priameia’ is the adjective from Priam agreeing with ‘coniunx’, “Priam's wife”. ‘post omnia’, “after everything”, counts the losses the rest of this part will show. ‘qua’ is the adverbial relative “where”, and ‘longus … Hellespontus’ is pulled apart around it while the strait itself is squeezed ‘in angustum’, “into a narrow”.

sentences.t: Ilion ardebat, neque adhuc consederat ignis,
sentences.l: Ilion was burning, and the fire had not yet settled,
sentences.i: Ilion was in flames, and the fire had not yet sunk down,
sentences.n: ‘Ilion’ is the Greek neuter name of the city. ‘consido’ is used of fire sinking and settling as it burns itself out. The imperfect ‘ardebat’ with the pluperfect ‘consederat’ holds the scene at one unfinished moment instead of moving it on.

sentences.t:
exiguumque senis Priami Iovis ara cruorem
combiberat tracta atque comis antistita Phoebi
non profecturas tendebat ad aethera palmas.
sentences.l: and the altar of Jupiter had drunk up the scant blood of old Priam, and, dragged by the hair, the priestess of Phoebus was stretching towards the upper air palms that would accomplish nothing.
sentences.i: and Jupiter's altar had drunk up what little blood old Priam had, and the priestess of Phoebus, dragged along by the hair, was stretching towards heaven hands that would win her nothing.
sentences.n: ‘exiguum’ opens 409 and its noun ‘cruorem’ closes the same line, with the genitives and the subject packed in between; the blood is scant because the man is old. ‘combiberat’ is “had drunk up”, of the altar. ‘antistita’ is the feminine of ‘antistes’, “priestess”: the text gives her office and her god, not her name. ‘tracta’, “dragged”, agrees with her, and ‘comis’ is the ablative telling by what. ‘non profecturas’ is a future participle of ‘proficio’ — hands that are going to achieve nothing. Magnus prints ‘tracta atque comis’, where ‘atque’ is postponed inside its own clause and joins ‘tendebat’ to ‘combiberat’; some editions print ‘tractata comis’, with no connective at all.

sentences.t:
Dardanidas matres patriorum signa deorum,
dum licet, amplexas succensaque templa tenentes
invidiosa trahunt victores praemia Grai.
sentences.l: The Dardanian mothers, who while it is allowed have embraced the images of their fathers' gods and are holding on to the kindled temples, the victorious Greeks drag away, prizes to be envied.
sentences.i: The Trojan mothers, clasping the images of their fathers' gods while they still may and clinging to the burning temples, the victorious Greeks drag off as prizes other men will envy.
sentences.n: ‘Dardanidas’ is a Greek accusative plural, “daughters of Dardanus”, i.e. the women of Troy. ‘amplexas’ is the perfect participle of the deponent ‘amplector’ and is active in sense, “having embraced”. ‘invidiosa … praemia’ stands in apposition to them: they are dragged off as prizes. The object ‘Dardanidas matres’ opens 412; in 414 the subject ‘victores … Grai’ is split around ‘praemia’, with the verb ‘trahunt’ standing ahead of the whole group and ‘invidiosa’ ahead of that, agreeing with ‘praemia’ across the line.

sentences.t:
Mittitur Astyanax illis de turribus, unde
pugnantem pro se proavitaque regna tuentem
saepe videre patrem monstratum a matre solebat.
sentences.l: Astyanax is sent from those towers, from which he used often to see his father — fighting for him and guarding the realms of his forefathers — pointed out by his mother.
sentences.i: Astyanax is sent down from the very towers from which he used so often to watch his father, pointed out to him by his mother, fighting on his behalf and defending the kingdom of his forefathers.
sentences.n: ‘Mittitur’, simply “is sent”, is the whole account of the child's death: the poem says only that he is sent from the towers and leaves the rest unsaid. ‘solebat’ with the infinitive ‘videre’, “he used to see”, sets the long habit against the single act. ‘monstratum a matre’ agrees with ‘patrem’ — it was his mother who used to point his father out to him from that same wall. ‘proavita regna’ are the realms of his great-grandfathers.

sentences.t:
Iamque viam suadet boreas, flatuque secundo
carbasa mota sonant, iubet uti navita ventis.
sentences.l: And now the north wind urges the voyage, and with a following blast the canvas, set moving, sounds; the sailor bids them use the winds.
sentences.i: And now the north wind advises sailing; the canvas stirs and cracks in the following breeze, and the sailing-master tells them to take the wind.
sentences.n: ‘boreas’ is the Greek name of the north wind, here standing as a noun and the subject of ‘suadet’. ‘carbasa’ is a neuter plural, the linen of the sails. ‘secundo’ of a wind is “following”, the sailor's word for favourable, not “second”. ‘uti’ is the deponent ‘utor’, which governs the ablative ‘ventis’. ‘navita’ is the poetic form of ‘nauta’.

sentences.t:
“Troia, vale! rapimur” clamant, dant oscula terrae
Troades et patriae fumantia tecta relinquunt.
sentences.l: “Troy, farewell! we are being snatched away,” they cry; the women of Troy give kisses to the earth and leave the smoking roofs of their fatherland.
sentences.i: “Troy, farewell! We are being torn away,” they cry; the Trojan women kiss the ground and leave the smoking roofs of home behind them.
sentences.n: ‘rapimur’ is passive, “we are being snatched away”; it is also the word used of being carried off by wind and tide, so it does double duty for the ship and for the captivity. ‘Troades’ is a Greek feminine plural, “the women of Troy”, and it is held back to the head of 421 although the two verbs it governs, ‘clamant’ and ‘dant’, have already run in 420. ‘patriae’ is genitive with ‘tecta’, “the roofs of their fatherland”.

sentences.t:
Ultima conscendit classem (miserabile visu!)
in mediis Hecube natorum inventa sepulcris:
sentences.l: Last she boarded the fleet — pitiable to see! — Hecuba, found in the midst of the tombs of her sons:
sentences.i: Last of all Hecuba came aboard — a pitiable sight — found among the graves of her children:
sentences.n: ‘Ultima’ is a predicative adjective where English wants an adverb: she goes aboard last. ‘miserabile visu’ has the supine ‘visu’, an ablative of respect — “pitiable in the seeing”. ‘Hecube’ is the Greek nominative of the queen's name; Magnus prints ‘Hecube’, where some editions print ‘Hecabe’. ‘inventa’, “found”, agrees with her, so the poem finds her before it names what she is doing.

sentences.t:
prensantem tumulos atque ossibus oscula dantem
Dulichiae traxere manus,
sentences.l: Her, clutching at the mounds and giving kisses to the bones, Dulichian hands dragged away,
sentences.i: Clutching at the burial mounds and pressing kisses on the bones, she was dragged away by Dulichian hands,
sentences.n: ‘traxere’ is the poetic third-person plural perfect for ‘traxerunt’, “they dragged”. The ‑ēre ending for ‑ērunt is standard in verse; this is its only occurrence in these lines. The participles ‘prensantem’ and ‘dantem’ agree with her as object, so the Latin holds her in the accusative for the whole of 424, and the verb arrives only as the second word of 425. ‘Dulichiae … manus’ names the men who take her by their island rather than by their commander.

sentences.t:
tamen unius hausit
inque sinu cineres secum tulit Hectoris haustos;
sentences.l: yet of one only she scooped some up, and in her bosom carried away with her the scooped-up ashes of Hector;
sentences.i: yet from one grave she snatched a handful, and carried away in her bosom the ashes she had scooped — Hector's;
sentences.n: ‘unius’ is genitive, “of one only”, and which one is withheld. ‘hausit’ and ‘haustos’ are the same verb twice over, “scooped up” and “scooped-up”; strictly ‘cineres … haustos’ is the object of ‘tulit’, and ‘hausit’ borrows it. The name ‘Hectoris’ does not arrive until the fifth of the six words of 426, and it stands again at the head of 427.

sentences.t:
Hectoris in tumulo canum de vertice crinem,
inferias inopes, crinem lacrimasque reliquit.
sentences.l: On Hector's mound, grey hair from the top of her head — poor offerings to the dead — hair and tears she left.
sentences.i: On Hector's grave she left grey hair from the crown of her head — beggarly offerings to the dead — hair and tears.
sentences.n: ‘canum’ is accusative and agrees with ‘crinem’ across the words between, “grey hair”; it cannot go with the ablative ‘vertice’, and ‘de vertice’ is “from the top of the head”. ‘inferias inopes’ is in apposition: ‘inferiae’ are the offerings made at a tomb to the dead, and ‘inopes’, “destitute”, says she has nothing else left to give. ‘crinem’ is then repeated to pick the sentence up again after the apposition.

sentences.t:
Est, ubi Troia fuit, Phrygiae contraria tellus,
Bistoniis habitata viris:
sentences.l: There is, where Troy was, a land lying opposite Phrygia, inhabited by Bistonian men:
sentences.i: Across from where Troy stood there is a land facing Phrygia, peopled by Bistonian men:
sentences.n: ‘Est’ at the head is the formula that opens a description of a place, “there is a land …”. ‘ubi Troia fuit’ is thrown in before ‘Phrygiae contraria’: the land lies opposite the place where Troy stood, not on it. ‘contraria’ takes the dative ‘Phrygiae’, “facing Phrygia”. ‘Bistoniis … viris’ is a bare ablative of agent with ‘habitata’, without the usual ‘a’; the Bistones are a Thracian people, and the king of this land is called ‘rex Thracum’ at 436.

sentences.t:
Polymestoris illic
regia dives erat,
sentences.l: there the rich palace of Polymestor was,
sentences.i: there stood the rich palace of Polymestor,
sentences.n: ‘regia’ here is the noun, “palace”, not the adjective. ‘dives’, “rich”, is the word the story turns on: the wealth named in this half-line becomes the motive at 433–434.

sentences.t:
cui te commisit alendum
clam, Polydore, pater Phrygiisque removit ab armis,
sentences.l: to whom your father entrusted you to be reared, secretly, Polydorus, and removed you from the Phrygian arms,
sentences.i: to whom your father secretly entrusted you, Polydorus, to be brought up, and so took you out of the fighting in Phrygia,
sentences.n: Ovid turns aside and speaks to the boy himself — ‘te’, and the vocative ‘Polydore’. This apostrophe is a habit of his: the sudden second person is not a change of speaker, and he will do it again at 483. ‘alendum’ is a gerundive of purpose after ‘commisit’, “handed you over to be reared”. ‘cui’ is the relative picking up Polymestor. ‘Phrygiis … armis’ is the war at Troy.

sentences.t:
consilium sapiens, sceleris nisi praemia magnas
adiecisset opes, animi inritamen avari.
sentences.l: a wise plan, had not the rewards of crime added great wealth, a goad to a greedy mind.
sentences.i: a wise plan — had not the wages of crime thrown in great riches with the boy, a goad for a greedy heart.
sentences.n: ‘consilium sapiens’ is in apposition to what the father did: “a wise plan”. ‘nisi … adiecisset’ is a pluperfect subjunctive and the condition is contrary to fact, so the plan was not wise after all. ‘sceleris … praemia’ is the subject, split around ‘nisi’, and ‘magnas … opes’ the object, split across the line-end. ‘inritamen’ is a rare noun, “a goad, a provocation”, in apposition to the wealth, with ‘animi … avari’ genitive, “of a greedy mind”.

sentences.t:
Ut cecidit fortuna Phrygum, capit impius ensem
rex Thracum iuguloque sui demisit alumni
et, tamquam tolli cum corpore crimina possent,
exanimem scopulo subiectas misit in undas.
sentences.l: When the fortune of the Phrygians fell, the impious king of the Thracians takes a sword and sank it into the throat of his own foster-son, and, as though crimes could be taken away along with the body, threw him lifeless from the crag into the waves beneath.
sentences.i: When Troy's fortune fell, the godless king of Thrace took a sword and drove it into the throat of the boy in his keeping, and then — as if guilt could be got rid of along with the body — flung the corpse from the crag into the sea below.
sentences.n: ‘capit’ is present and ‘demisit’ perfect within one sentence, the alternation that hurries an action and then fixes it; both come into English as past. ‘impius’ is the exact reverse of ‘pius’: he breaks the bond that made the boy his charge. ‘alumni’, “foster-son”, is the poem's word for the boy he was rearing, and it is what makes this a crime inside his own house. ‘tamquam … possent’ is an imperfect subjunctive in an unreal comparison, “as though they could be”. ‘subiectas … undas’ are the waves lying below; ‘scopulo’ is taken here as the ablative of the rock he threw him from, and it can equally be read as the dative with ‘subiectas’, “the waves lying beneath the crag”.

sentences.t:
Litore Threicio classem religarat Atrides,
dum mare pacatum, dum ventus amicior esset.
sentences.l: On the Thracian shore the son of Atreus had moored his fleet, until the sea should be calm, until the wind should be friendlier.
sentences.i: The son of Atreus had tied up his fleet on the Thracian shore, waiting for the sea to settle and the wind to turn kinder.
sentences.n: ‘religarat’ is the syncopated pluperfect for ‘religaverat’; the edition keeps these shortened forms and they are not errors. ‘Atrides’ is a Greek patronymic, “son of Atreus”; the man is named at 444. ‘dum … esset’ with the subjunctive is “until it should be”, of waiting for something to come about, and ‘dum’ is repeated for the two things waited for.

sentences.t:
Hic subito, quantus cum viveret esse solebat,
exit humo late rupta similisque minanti
temporis illius vultum referebat Achilles,
sentences.l: Here suddenly, as great as he used to be while he was alive, Achilles comes out of the ground broken wide open, and, like a man making a threat, was bringing back the face of that time,
sentences.i: Here suddenly, as tall as he had been in life, Achilles came up out of the ground as it split wide open, and, with the look of a man about to strike, wore again the face he had worn at the moment
sentences.n: ‘quantus … esse solebat’, “as great as he used to be”, is a correlative with its ‘tantus’ left unexpressed. ‘humo late rupta’ is the ablative of separation with ‘exit’, “out of the ground”, with ‘late rupta’, “broken wide open”, agreeing with ‘humo’: the ground splits as he comes. It can also be read as an ablative absolute, leaving ‘exit’ without an expressed source. ‘similis’ takes the dative ‘minanti’, “like a man making a threat”. ‘referebat’ is “brought back, reproduced” — the face itself returns. The subject ‘Achilles’ is withheld to the last word of 443, so the reader learns who this is only at the end.

sentences.t: quo ferus iniustum petiit Agamemnona ferro,
sentences.l: at which, savage, he made for unjust Agamemnon with the iron,
sentences.i: when, in his fury, he went for Agamemnon in the wrong with the sword,
sentences.n: ‘quo’ is a relative in the ablative of time picking up ‘temporis illius’ in 443 — “at which time”. ‘Agamemnona’ is a Greek accusative singular in ‑a. ‘ferus’ is predicative of the subject, “savage as he was”, and ‘iniustum’ is not a neutral epithet either: the line judges the old quarrel in both directions at once, calling Achilles savage and Agamemnon in the wrong, and English should keep both charges rather than smooth them. ‘ferro’, literally “with iron”, is the ordinary word for a sword.

sentences.t:
“inmemores” que “mei disceditis” inquit “Achivi,
obrutaque est mecum virtutis gratia nostrae?
sentences.l: “Forgetful of me,” he says, “do you go away, Achaeans, and has the thanks for our valour been buried along with me?
sentences.i: “Do you sail away forgetting me, Achaeans,” he said, “and has all thanks for my courage been buried with me?
sentences.n: ‘inmemores’ is the edition's unassimilated spelling for ‘immemores’, and the adjective takes the genitive ‘mei’, “forgetful of me”. The enclitic ‘-que’ is printed outside the quotation mark: it joins ‘inquit’ to ‘referebat’ in 443, and the quotation is broken open to let ‘inquit’ in. ‘gratia’ here is the thanks owed for a service rendered, not charm. ‘nostrae’ is the poetic plural for singular: the literal keeps the Latin's “our”, but one man's valour is meant.

sentences.t:
Ne facite! utque meum non sit sine honore sepulcrum,
placet Achilleos mactata Polyxena manes!”
sentences.l: Do not do it! and, so that my tomb may not be without honour, let Polyxena, slaughtered, appease the shade of Achilles!”
sentences.i: Do not! And so that my tomb shall not go unhonoured, let Polyxena be sacrificed and appease Achilles' shade!”
sentences.n: ‘Ne facite’ is a prohibition with ‘ne’ and the plain imperative, blunter and older than ‘nolite facere’. ‘placet’ looks like the indicative of ‘placeo’, “it pleases”, but it is the present subjunctive of ‘placo’, “appease”, which is why it governs the accusative ‘manes’; it is jussive — “let her appease”. ‘mactata’, “sacrificed”, agrees with Polyxena and carries the whole act in one participle. ‘Achilleos’ is the accusative plural of the adjective ‘Achilleus’, “of Achilles”, agreeing with ‘manes’: he names himself and speaks of himself in the third person.

sentences.t:
Dixit, et inmiti sociis parentibus umbrae,
rapta sinu matris, quam iam prope sola fovebat,
fortis et infelix et plus quam femina virgo
ducitur ad tumulum diroque fit hostia busto.
sentences.l: He spoke, and — his companions obeying the pitiless shade — snatched from the bosom of her mother, whom now almost alone she was comforting, the maiden, brave and unhappy and more than a woman, is led to the mound and becomes a victim at the dreadful pyre.
sentences.i: He spoke, and his companions obeyed the pitiless ghost. Torn from the arms of the mother whom she was now almost the only one left to comfort, the girl — brave and ill-starred and more than a woman — is led to the mound and made a sacrifice at that grim pyre.
sentences.n: ‘parentibus’ is the present participle of ‘pareo’, “obeying”, not the noun “parents”: ‘sociis parentibus’ is an ablative absolute with ‘inmiti … umbrae’ as its dative object, “his companions obeying the pitiless shade”. ‘inmiti’ is again the edition's unassimilated spelling. In ‘quam … fovebat’ the antecedent is the mother and the subject is the girl — she was almost the last comfort left. ‘hostia’ is the word for a sacrificial animal, used of her without softening. ‘busto’ is taken here as an ablative of place; it can also be read as a dative, “a victim to the grim tomb”.

sentences.t:
Quae memor ipsa sui, postquam crudelibus aris
admota est sensitque sibi fera sacra parari,
sentences.l: And she, mindful of her own self, after she had been brought up to the cruel altars and had felt that a savage rite was being made ready against her,
sentences.i: And she, keeping in mind who she was, once she had been brought up to the cruel altar and understood that a savage rite was being prepared for her,
sentences.n: ‘Quae’ opens the sentence as a connecting relative — “and she”. ‘memor’ takes the genitive ‘sui’, “mindful of herself”, of who she is and what is owed to it; the whole speech that follows grows out of these two words. ‘sensit … parari’ is an accusative and infinitive with a passive infinitive, “felt that a rite was being prepared”, and ‘sibi’ is the dative of the person it is being prepared against. ‘aris’ is a poetic plural for a single altar.

sentences.t:
utque Neoptolemum stantem ferrumque tenentem
utque suo vidit figentem lumina vultu,
utere iamdudum generoso sanguine!” dixit,
sentences.l: and when she saw Neoptolemus standing and holding the iron, and when she saw him fixing his eyes on her own face, “Use the noble blood, and long since!” she said,
sentences.i: and when she saw Neoptolemus standing there with the blade in his hand, and saw him fix his eyes on her face, “Make use of my noble blood,” she said, “you have waited long enough,”
sentences.n: ‘utere’ is the imperative of the deponent ‘utor’, which takes the ablative ‘generoso sanguine’; ‘iamdudum’ with an imperative means “this long while now”, that is, “and you should have done it already”. ‘utque … utque’ repeats the temporal clause; Magnus prints ‘utque’ at the head of 456, where some editions print ‘inque’, which would attach ‘in suo … vultu’ to ‘figentem’ instead. ‘suo … vultu’ is a bare ablative of place and ‘suo’ points back to her, the subject of ‘vidit’. The edition as archived prints the closing quotation mark at 457 with no opening one anywhere before it; the speech in fact begins at ‘utere’.

sentences.t:
“nulla mora est: aut tu iugulo vel pectore telum
conde meo!
sentences.l: “there is no delay: either in my throat or in my breast bury the weapon!
sentences.i: “There is no holding back on my side: bury the blade in my throat or in my breast!
sentences.n: ‘nulla mora est’ is “there is no delay” — she refuses to be the one holding anything up. ‘conde’ is the imperative of ‘condo’, “bury, sink”, the regular verb for driving a weapon home. ‘meo’ is held over to 459 and belongs with ‘iugulo’ in the line before, the two nouns sharing the one adjective. ‘aut … vel’ mixes the two disjunctives; Magnus prints ‘aut’, where some editions print ‘at’, “but”.

sentences.t:
(iugulumque simul pectusque retexit)
scilicet haud ulli servire Polyxena vellem.
sentences.l: (and she uncovered throat and breast at once) of course I, Polyxena, would be willing to be a slave to no one.
sentences.i: (and with that she bared her throat and her breast) “Of course I, Polyxena, would never consent to be any man's slave.
sentences.n: The bracket is the poem's own aside, breaking into her speech to report the gesture; the speech resumes at ‘scilicet’. ‘retexit’ is “uncovers, lays bare”, the opposite of ‘tego’. ‘servire’ takes the dative ‘ulli’, “be a slave to anyone”. ‘vellem’ is an imperfect subjunctive of the kind that states what one would want, and she sets her own name in the nominative beside the first-person verb, naming herself as she refuses.

sentences.t: haud per tale sacrum numen placabitis ullum!
sentences.l: by no such rite will you appease any divine power!
sentences.i: you will placate no god at all by a rite like this!
sentences.n: ‘haud … ullum’ is “not … any”, which English says as “no … at all”: ‘numen … ullum’ is the object of ‘placabitis’ and is split around the verb. ‘numen’ is a god's power to act rather than the god's person. ‘placabitis’ is future — she is telling them what the sacrifice will fail to accomplish, and the verb is the same one the ghost used at 448.

sentences.t: Mors tantum vellem matrem mea fallere posset!
sentences.l: I could only wish that my death were able to escape the notice of my mother!
sentences.i: I only wish my death could be kept from my mother!
sentences.n: ‘vellem’ is again the imperfect subjunctive of wishing, “I could wish”, and it governs ‘posset’ directly, without ‘ut’. ‘fallere’ with an accusative person is “to escape the notice of”, not “to deceive” by lying. ‘mors … mea’ is split around ‘tantum vellem matrem’, so the subject is not complete until the fifth word of the line.

sentences.t:
Mater obest minuitque necis mihi gaudia, quamvis
non mea mors illi, verum sua vita gemenda est.
sentences.l: My mother is in the way, and lessens for me the joys of a violent death, although not my death is to be lamented by her, but her own life.
sentences.i: My mother stands in the way and cuts down the joy I take in being killed — though it is not my dying she should mourn, but her own living.
sentences.n: ‘obest’ is ‘obsum’, “stands in the way, is an obstacle”. ‘necis’ is ‘nex’, a violent death, not the ordinary ‘mors’, and she speaks of its ‘gaudia’, “joys”, without irony: dying is what she wants. ‘gemenda est’ is a gerundive of obligation with ‘illi’ as the dative of agent, “must be mourned by her”. Magnus prints ‘gemenda’; some editions print ‘tremenda’, “to be dreaded”.

sentences.t:
Vos modo, ne Stygios adeam non libera manes,
ite procul, si iusta peto, tactuque viriles
virgineo removete manus!
sentences.l: You only — so that I may not go to the Stygian shades not free — stand far off, if what I ask is just, and take male hands away from a maiden's touch!
sentences.i: Only stand well back, so that I may not go down to the shades of Styx unfree; if my request is just, keep men's hands from touching a maiden!
sentences.n: ‘ne … adeam’ is a purpose clause, and ‘non libera’, “not free”, is her whole argument: what she refuses is a slave's death, not death. ‘tactu virgineo’ is an ablative of separation with ‘removete’, “away from a maiden's touch”. ‘viriles’ ends 466 and ‘virgineo’ opens 467, so the two adjectives, “male” and “maiden's”, stand side by side across the line-break while their nouns are pulled apart.

sentences.t:
Acceptior illi,
quisquis is est, quem caede mea placare paratis,
liber erit sanguis.
sentences.l: More acceptable to him — whoever he is, whom you are getting ready to appease with my slaughter — will free blood be.
sentences.i: The blood will be more welcome to him, whoever he is that you mean to appease by butchering me, if it is free blood.
sentences.n: The subject ‘liber … sanguis’ is held back to the end of the sentence, so the point — that it must be free blood — lands last. ‘quisquis is est’ is contempt, not ignorance: she will not name the shade the rite is for, though the poem named him at 443. ‘caede mea’ uses ‘caedes’, the word for butchery and slaughter, of her own death. ‘acceptior’ is the comparative of ‘acceptus’, “welcome”, with the dative ‘illi’.

sentences.t:
Siquos tamen ultima nostri
verba movent oris (Priami vos filia regis,
nunc captiva rogat), genetrici corpus inemptum
reddite,
sentences.l: If, however, the last words of our mouth move any of you — the daughter of king Priam, now a captive, asks you — give back to my mother the body unbought,
sentences.i: But if the last words of my lips move any of you — it is King Priam's daughter, now a captive, who asks — give my body back to my mother unbought,
sentences.n: ‘Siquos’ is ‘si quos’, “if any”, printed as one word. ‘nostri … oris’ is a poetic plural for singular, “of my mouth”. ‘Priami … filia regis’ is split around ‘vos’, the object of ‘rogat’, so those she is asking stand inside her own title. ‘genetrici’ is the dative, “to her who bore me”. ‘inemptum’, “unbought”, is the word the next sentence turns on. The collation against the second witness records no reading at all for 469; what that means about the witness has not been checked, and Magnus's line is printed as it stands.

sentences.t:
neve auro redimat ius triste sepulcri,
sed lacrimis!
sentences.l: and let her not buy back the sad right of a tomb with gold, but with tears!
sentences.i: and do not make her purchase the grim right of burial with gold, but with tears!
sentences.n: ‘neve’ carries the command ‘reddite’ on into a negative, “and let her not …”, with ‘redimat’ in the subjunctive. ‘auro’ and ‘lacrimis’ are ablatives of price. ‘ius … sepulcri’ is the right to bury a body — a thing that in this world has to be paid for, which is what makes it ‘triste’.

sentences.t: Tunc, cum poterat, redimebat et auro.”
sentences.l: Then, when she could, she used to buy back with gold as well.”
sentences.i: In the days when she could, she would pay in gold as well.”
sentences.n: The subject is still the mother of 471. ‘Tunc’ points back to the time when the house still had gold to give, and the imperfect ‘redimebat’ makes it a habit rather than one act. ‘et auro’ is “with gold as well”, set against the ‘lacrimis’ that are all she can pay with now. Magnus prints ‘Tunc’ where some editions print ‘tum’, with no difference in sense.

sentences.t:
Dixerat, at populus lacrimas, quas illa tenebat,
non tenet;
sentences.l: She had spoken; but the people does not hold back the tears which she was holding back;
sentences.i: She had finished; but the crowd could not hold back the tears that she held back;
sentences.n: ‘Dixerat’ is a pluperfect closing the speech off, set against the present ‘non tenet’. The same verb serves for both, ‘tenebat’ of her and ‘tenet’ of the crowd; ‘lacrimas’ stands ahead of both as the object of ‘non tenet’, and the relative ‘quas’ picks it up as the object of ‘tenebat’. ‘populus’ is a collective noun and takes a singular verb.

sentences.t:
ipse etiam flens invitusque sacerdos
praebita coniecto rupit praecordia ferro.
sentences.l: the priest himself too, weeping and unwilling, broke open with the driven iron the breast that was held out to him.
sentences.i: the priest himself, weeping and against his will, drove the blade in and broke open the breast she offered him.
sentences.n: ‘praebita … praecordia’ is “the breast held out”, from ‘praebeo’: she offered it, and the participle records that she did. ‘coniecto … ferro’ is an ablative absolute doing the work of an instrument, “the iron having been driven in”. ‘praecordia’ is a plural noun for the midriff, the parts lying about the heart. ‘sacerdos’ names the killer by his ritual office — the man standing with the blade at 455 — and ‘flens invitusque’ says plainly that he did not want to do what the office required.

sentences.t:
Illa super terram defecto poplite labens
pertulit intrepidos ad fata novissima vultus.
sentences.l: She, sinking down onto the ground with her knee giving way, carried through to her last moments a face that did not flinch.
sentences.i: She sank to the ground, her knee giving under her, and carried a fearless face through to the very end.
sentences.n: ‘defecto poplite’ is an ablative absolute, “her knee having given way”; ‘poples’ is properly the back of the knee. ‘novissima’ is the ordinary Latin for “last”, not “newest”, so ‘fata novissima’ are her final moments. ‘vultus’ is a plural used of one face, and ‘pertulit’ is “carried it right through”. ‘intrepidos’ is the poem's own judgement on her, agreeing with ‘vultus’.

sentences.t:
Tunc quoque cura fuit partes velare tegendas,
cum caderet, castique decus servare pudoris.
sentences.l: Then too it was her care to veil the parts that must be covered, as she was falling, and to keep the honour of chaste modesty.
sentences.i: Even then, as she fell, she took care to cover what should be covered, and to keep the dignity of an untouched modesty.
sentences.n: ‘quoque’ here is the adverb, “too”; the same letters can be ‘quo‑que’, “and by which”, and it is worth checking each time which it is. ‘partes … tegendas’ is a gerundive, “the parts that must be covered” — the Latin identifies them no further than that. ‘cum caderet’, with the imperfect subjunctive, is dropped in between the two infinitives that depend on ‘cura fuit’. ‘decus … pudoris’ is the standing that modesty confers, and she is still defending it as she falls.

sentences.t:
Troades excipiunt deploratosque recensent
Priamidas et quid dederit domus una cruoris,
sentences.l: The women of Troy take her up and count over the lamented sons of Priam, and how much of blood one house has given,
sentences.i: The women of Troy take her up, and reckon up the sons of Priam they have mourned, and how much blood a single house has yielded,
sentences.n: ‘excipiunt’ is “catch, take up” — they take up her body, which 477–478 have already brought to the ground. ‘Priamidas’ is a Greek accusative plural patronymic, “the sons of Priam”, with ‘deploratos’, “wept for”, agreeing. ‘quid … cruoris’ is a partitive genitive, “how much of blood”, and ‘dederit’ is subjunctive because the question is indirect. Magnus prints ‘quid … cruoris’; some editions print ‘quot … cruores’, “how many bloodsheds”.

sentences.t:
teque gemunt, virgo, teque, o modo regia coniunx,
regia dicta parens, Asiae florentis imago,
sentences.l: and they groan for you, maiden, and for you, o lately a royal wife, called a royal mother, image of Asia in flower,
sentences.i: and they weep for you, girl, and for you who were lately a king's wife and were called a king's mother, the very image of Asia in her flowering,
sentences.n: The poem turns from narrating to addressing, ‘te … te’, first the girl and then the queen — the woman named at 423 — just as it turned to Polydorus at 432. ‘modo’ is “only just now”, and both ‘regia’s belong to a past that has closed: royal wife, and called royal mother. ‘Asiae florentis imago’ makes her the figure of a whole continent at its height, ‘florentis’ being a present participle used as an adjective.

sentences.t:
nunc etiam praedae mala sors, quam victor Ulixes
esse suam nollet, nisi quod tamen Hectora partu
edideras:
sentences.l: now even the bad lot of the plunder, whom the victor Ulysses would not wish to be his own, except that you had nevertheless brought forth Hector in childbirth:
sentences.i: and now even a bad share of the spoil, whom Ulysses in his victory would not want for his own, but that you had after all borne Hector:
sentences.n: ‘praedae mala sors’ is “the bad lot of the plunder”: she is a share in the spoil, and the share nobody wants. The words are the poem's and are not softened here. ‘sors’ is the lot as drawn or allotted. ‘nollet’ is a potential imperfect subjunctive, “would not want”. ‘nisi quod’ is “except for the fact that”. ‘Hectora’ is a Greek accusative in ‑a, and ‘partu edideras’, “you had brought forth in childbirth”, keeps the second person of the address.

sentences.t: dominum matri vix repperit Hector!
sentences.l: Hector barely found a master for his mother!
sentences.i: Hector could scarcely find his mother an owner!
sentences.n: ‘dominum’ is the master of a slave, and the sentence says outright what she has become: a woman whose one remaining value among the spoils is the son she bore. ‘vix repperit’, “scarcely found”, is bitter, not admiring. The name closes 487 in the nominative after standing in the accusative, ‘Hectora’, in 486.

sentences.t:
Quae corpus complexa animae tam fortis inane,
quas totiens patriae dederat natisque viroque,
huic quoque dat lacrimas
sentences.l: And she, having embraced the body empty of a soul so brave, gives to this one too the tears which she had so often given to her country and to her sons and to her husband.
sentences.i: And she, embracing the body emptied of so brave a spirit, gives to her too the tears she had given so often to her country, to her sons, to her husband.
sentences.n: ‘Quae’ is again a connecting relative, “and she”, and ‘complexa’ again a deponent participle active in sense, as ‘amplexas’ was at 413. ‘inane’ takes the genitive ‘animae … fortis’, “empty of a soul so brave”. The relative ‘quas’ stands in 489 before its own antecedent ‘lacrimas’, which does not arrive until 490. The repeated ‘-que … -que’ piles the losses one on another.

sentences.t:
lacrimas in vulnera fundit
osculaque ore tegit consuetaque pectora plangit
canitiemque suam concreto in sanguine verrens
plura quidem, sed et haec laniato pectore dixit:
sentences.l: she pours tears into the wounds, and covers her lips with her own mouth, and beats the breast she is used to beating, and, sweeping her own white hair in the clotted blood, more things indeed, but this too, with her breast torn, she said:
sentences.i: she pours tears into the wounds and covers her lips with her own mouth and beats the breast she has beaten so often; and, trailing her white hair through the clotted blood, she said much more, but this among it, her breast torn:
sentences.n: The edition as archived prints no stop between the two ‘lacrimas’ in 490: the first is the object of ‘dat’, the second of ‘fundit’, and the word is repeated across the join. In ‘oscula … tegit’ the accusative ‘oscula’ is the object of ‘tegit’ and so is the thing covered: ‘osculum’ is properly a little mouth, and the sense is that she lays her own mouth, ‘ore’, over the dead girl's lips. Read as “kisses” instead, the accusative would leave ‘tegit’ with nothing to cover. ‘consueta … pectora’ is taken here as her own breast, the one she has beaten so often; it can also be read as the girl's, familiar to her. ‘verrens’ is a present participle hanging on ‘dixit’ at the end of 493, and ‘laniato pectore’ is an ablative absolute — the tearing is her own doing. Magnus prints ‘concreto in sanguine verrens’; some editions print ‘concretam’, making the hair itself clotted, and ‘vellens’, “tearing”, for ‘verrens’.
